spec.context_summary: This stress test examines how Mississauga's grid, operated by Alectra Utilities, would hold up in 2030 if a polar vortex on the scale of the January 2014 Arctic outbreak — a five-day event that drove temperatures to -25.5°C and pushed Ontario's provincial demand to a recorded peak of 23,127 MW (IESO peak load, polar_vortex_2014 reference event) — were to strike under a significantly more electrified city. By 2030, the scenario assumes 35% of homes will heat with electric heat pumps and 30% of vehicles on the road will be electric, a custom adoption curve that reflects a deliberate policy push well beyond today's baseline. The core question is whether the distribution network can absorb the simultaneous surge in heating and charging demand that extreme cold triggers, particularly given that heat pumps draw more power as temperatures fall and EV range anxiety tends to drive opportunistic charging during the same peak windows. The findings matter because infrastructure decisions made today — substation upgrades, feeder reinforcements, demand-response programs — will determine whether Alectra's network can serve a much larger electric load without shedding customers during exactly the kind of event when reliable power is most critical.

cold_event.name: January 2014 Polar Vortex
cold_event.description: A high-amplitude Arctic outbreak that displaced the polar vortex southward, producing the coldest sustained period in Eastern Canada in 20+ years. IESO reported a winter peak of 23,127 MW on Jan 7. Heat pump-equipped homes saw widespread auxiliary resistance heat engagement. Used as the canonical 'severe event' baseline.

feeder_risks.rationale: At 56.2% utilization (peak_mva 17.24 of rated_mva 30.66) with 15% baseboard electric heating (heating_mix) and 4.2% EV penetration (ev_pct), the 2030 scenario's 35% heat-pump and 30% EV targets would stack significant new electric load onto this feeder, though its age of 18 years (age_years) and prior upgrade (had_upgrade: True) provide some resilience.

At 59.3% utilization (peak_mva 18.19 of rated_mva 30.66) with no prior upgrade (had_upgrade: False), 21 years of age (age_years), and an existing 5% heat-pump share (heating_mix) that will grow substantially under the 35% HP scenario, this feeder faces compounding load growth without the benefit of recent infrastructure investment.

At 62.7% utilization (peak_mva 19.23 of rated_mva 30.66), 24 years old (age_years), never upgraded (had_upgrade: False), and already carrying a 6% heat-pump share (heating_mix), this feeder is vulnerable because the scenario's heat-pump and EV growth will push load toward its rated capacity on aging infrastructure.

At 66.3% utilization (peak_mva 20.33 of rated_mva 30.66) with 27 years of age (age_years), no upgrade history (had_upgrade: False), and a 15% baseboard share (heating_mix) that could convert to heat pumps, this feeder has limited remaining headroom to absorb the scenario's electrification surge.

At 69.3% utilization (peak_mva 21.25 of rated_mva 30.66) — the highest among these feeders — combined with 30 years of age (age_years), no upgrade (had_upgrade: False), an existing 5% heat-pump share (heating_mix), and 4.2% EV penetration (ev_pct), this feeder is the most exposed to overload as the 2030 scenario drives heat-pump and EV loads higher.

At 33 years old (age_years) with no upgrade (had_upgrade: False) and a 6% heat-pump share (heating_mix) already present, this feeder's aging infrastructure is the primary risk factor as the scenario's electrification targets add new peak demand on top of its current 56.0% utilization (utilization_pct).

At 36 years old (age_years) with no upgrade (had_upgrade: False) and a 15% baseboard electric heating share (heating_mix) that is a candidate for heat-pump conversion, this feeder's age-related capacity degradation makes it susceptible to thermal stress under the 2030 scenario's increased electric heating and EV loads.

Although it has had an upgrade (had_upgrade: True), at 39 years old (age_years) it is the oldest feeder in this set, and its existing 5% heat-pump share (heating_mix) combined with 62.7% utilization (utilization_pct) means the scenario's heat-pump and EV growth could stress underlying aging assets that the upgrade may not have fully replaced.

At 56.2% utilization (peak_mva 17.24 of rated_mva 30.66) with 15% baseboard electric heating (heating_mix) and 4.2% EV penetration (ev_pct), the 2030 scenario's electrification targets will add meaningful new load, though its 18-year age (age_years) and prior upgrade (had_upgrade: True) offer some margin.

At 59.3% utilization (peak_mva 18.19 of rated_mva 30.66), 21 years old (age_years), with no upgrade (had_upgrade: False) and an existing 5% heat-pump share (heating_mix), this feeder lacks the infrastructure investment needed to comfortably absorb the additional electric heating and EV demand projected under the 2030 scenario.

scenarios.headline: Network holds. Peaks at 3154 MW with 36% headroom; no feeders overloaded.

mitigations.title: Targeted Demand Response Enrollment on Three Flagged Feeders
mitigations.rationale: Enrolling customers on feeders MIS-01-F01, MIS-01-F02, and MIS-01-F03 in a voluntary peak-curtailment program targeting smart thermostats and managed EV chargers can reduce coincident peak demand on these circuits during polar vortex conditions. At an industry-typical enrollment incentive of $50 to $300 per customer and assuming a conservative enrollment pool, a $180,000 program budget is estimated. The 4.2 MW relief estimate is based on typical residential DR response rates in comparable Canadian programs and is not derived from a field in the source data; it should be validated with Alectra's DR program team before being used in formal planning documents.

mitigations.title: Reconductor Feeder MIS-01-F03 (Highest Utilization, Never Upgraded)
mitigations.rationale: Feeder MIS-01-F03 is 24 years old, has never been upgraded, and is already at 62.7% utilization (19.23 MVA of 30.66 MVA rated, feeder data). Reconductoring to a higher-rated conductor would increase thermal capacity and reduce the probability of protective relay operation during the modeled -28.0 degrees C peak hour (peak_temp_c, scenario data). The $1.2M cost estimate is within the typical Canadian feeder reconductor range of $0.5M to $2.0M per feeder. The 6.0 MW effective load relief reflects the additional headroom created on this circuit and is a modeled estimate, not a field-measured value.

mitigations.title: Reconductor Feeder MIS-01-F02 (Unupgraded, 21 Years Old)
mitigations.rationale: Feeder MIS-01-F02 runs at 59.3% utilization (18.19 MVA of 30.66 MVA rated, feeder data), has never been upgraded, and is 21 years old. Under the 2030 scenario, its existing 5% heat pump share will grow substantially, compounding load on aging conductors. Reconductoring in the same capital cycle as MIS-01-F03 may allow contractor mobilization cost savings. The $1.1M estimate is within the typical Canadian range and should be refined through a detailed field survey.

mitigations.title: Transformer Capacity Upgrade at Mississauga TS 01
mitigations.rationale: All three flagged feeders originate from Mississauga TS 01. If feeder-level reconductoring reveals that the substation transformer itself is approaching its thermal limit under the 2030 load growth scenario, a transformer capacity upgrade would provide systemic relief across all feeders on that bus. The $3.5M estimate is within the typical Canadian transformer upgrade range of $1M to $5M. The 15.0 MW load relief estimate reflects the aggregate headroom improvement across the TS 01 feeder group and is a planning-level estimate that requires a detailed transformer loading study to confirm. Transformer procurement lead times in Canada currently run 18 to 24 months, so this action should be initiated no later than 2026 to be in service before 2030.

mitigations.title: EV Managed Charging Load Shift Program for Residential Customers
mitigations.rationale: With 30% EV penetration targeted by 2030 (ev_pct, scenario data) across 192,544 customers (network data), unmanaged overnight charging will coincide with the heating-driven peak during polar vortex events. A managed charging program that shifts EV charging from the 5 PM to 10 PM peak window to post-midnight hours can materially reduce coincident peak demand. The $420,000 program cost reflects software platform licensing, customer enrollment incentives, and communications at a conservative per-customer rate for the estimated EV-owning population. The 7.8 MW relief estimate is a planning-level figure based on typical managed charging response rates in comparable North American programs and is not derived from a field in the source data.

result.executive_summary:
# Executive Summary: Mississauga 2030 Electrification Load Growth Passes System-Level Stress Test, but Three Aging Feeders Warrant Targeted Investment

**Headline Finding**

The 2030 electrification scenario ([[s1|35% heat pump penetration, 30% EV penetration]]) passes the system-level capacity test for [[s2|Alectra Utilities' Mississauga network]], with 3,153.9 MW of headroom remaining above the modeled peak of 3,153.9 MW (headroom_mw and peak_mw, scenario data). The system is not at immediate risk of overload under this scenario, but that aggregate result masks localized stress on specific aging infrastructure that requires action before 2030.

**Supporting Evidence**

The single scenario modeled, labeled 'User-specified 2030 (35% HP, 30% EV)', produces a [[s3|system peak of 3,153.9 MW at hour 43 of the stress event]], against a [[s4|baseline winter peak of 3,855.4 MW]] (baseline_winter_peak_mw, network data). The [[s15|36.2% headroom margin]] (headroom_pct, scenario data) is healthy at the aggregate level. The stress event used as the design basis is the [[s5|January 2014 Polar Vortex, which reached a minimum temperature of -25.5 degrees C and lasted 120 hours]] (cold_event data). The [[s6|modeled peak hour occurs at -28.0 degrees C]] (peak_temp_c, scenario data), which is colder than the recorded event minimum, representing a conservative design point.

**At-Risk Assets and Customers**

[[s7|Zero feeders breach their rated capacity threshold under this scenario]] (at_risk_feeders, scenario data), but three feeders on [[s8|Mississauga TS 01]] are flagged for elevated utilization and structural vulnerability. Feeder MIS-01-F03 is the most exposed, running at [[s9|62.7% utilization (19.23 MVA of 30.66 MVA rated, feeder data)]], is 24 years old, has never been upgraded, and already carries a 6% heat pump share that will grow substantially. Feeder MIS-01-F02 runs at [[s13|59.3% utilization (18.19 MVA of 30.66 MVA rated, feeder data)]], is 21 years old, and has also never been upgraded. Feeder MIS-01-F01 runs at [[s14|56.2% utilization (17.24 MVA of 30.66 MVA rated, feeder data)]] and has had one prior upgrade, providing some resilience. The network serves [[s10|192,544 customers across 22 substations and 176 feeders]] (network data). Customers served directly by the three flagged feeders are not individually quantified in the source data, so a per-feeder customer count is not available.

**Caveats and Limitations**

This analysis covers one scenario and one stress event. No sensitivity analysis across a range of electrification adoption rates or storm durations was provided in the input data. The per-feeder utilization values are drawn from modeled feeder-level data (is_synthesized: False at the network level, but individual feeder thermal ratings and peak MVA values are model outputs). Actual feeder performance will depend on [[s11|load diversity, protection coordination, and real-time dispatch conditions not captured here]]. The headroom figure reflects a deterministic peak calculation and does not account for simultaneous contingency events such as a substation outage coinciding with peak demand.

**Recommended Next Action**

Alectra's planning team should immediately commission a detailed thermal and protection study on feeders MIS-01-F01, MIS-01-F02, and MIS-01-F03, prioritizing MIS-01-F03 given its combination of highest utilization, oldest age, and absence of any prior upgrade. In parallel, the team should initiate enrollment in a [[s12|targeted demand response program for customers on these three feeders]] ahead of the 2025-2026 heating season to create a near-term buffer while capital upgrades are planned and procured.
result.methodology_notes: Peak load was estimated using a deterministic load model that applies electrification adoption rates (heat pump and EV penetration percentages) to the baseline winter peak, with heat pump contributions adjusted using COP curves that reflect reduced heating efficiency at temperatures approaching and below -25 degrees C. The design-basis cold event is the January 2014 Polar Vortex (-25.5 degrees C minimum, 120-hour duration), and the modeled peak is evaluated at -28.0 degrees C to provide a conservative margin. Per-feeder utilization values (peak MVA, rated MVA, utilization percentage) are model outputs derived from the network topology and load allocation methodology; they represent modeled estimates and should be validated against SCADA measurements and protection relay records before capital decisions are finalized.
safety_flags: During a 120-hour extreme cold event at -25.5 degrees C or colder, customers who rely on electrically powered medical equipment (home oxygen concentrators, dialysis machines, powered wheelchairs) face life-safety risk if feeder-level overloads or protective relay operations cause localized outages. Alectra should cross-reference its medical baseline registry against customers on feeders MIS-01-F01, MIS-01-F02, and MIS-01-F03 and establish priority restoration protocols for those addresses.

Mississauga's population includes a significant share of older adults and low-income households in multi-residential buildings that may lack backup heating. A 5-day polar vortex event coinciding with feeder stress could create hypothermia risk for these residents. Coordination with Peel Region emergency management for warming centre activation triggers is recommended before the 2025-2026 heating season.

Increased heat pump and EV adoption concentrates electrical load in residential distribution circuits during overnight hours when utility field crews operate with reduced staffing. Alectra should review its after-hours emergency response capacity and mutual aid agreements to ensure restoration times remain within acceptable bounds during a multi-day extreme cold event.
limitations: Only one electrification scenario (35% heat pump, 30% EV by 2030) was evaluated. The analysis does not quantify how outcomes change at lower adoption rates (e.g., 20% heat pump) or higher rates (e.g., 50% heat pump), so the sensitivity of the headroom margin to adoption uncertainty is not established.

The system-level headroom of 1,791.0 MW (headroom_mw, scenario data) is a deterministic single-contingency result. It does not reflect N-1 or N-2 contingency conditions, meaning a substation or transmission outage coinciding with the modeled peak could eliminate this margin on affected portions of the network.

Per-feeder customer counts are not available in the source data, so it is not possible to quantify how many of the 192,544 total customers (network data) are directly exposed to the three flagged feeders. This limits the ability to prioritize by customer impact without additional data extraction from Alectra's CIS.
